There were 2 issues that needed to be overcome. The library first creates the databases, then looks for extensions (does not find them), then runs the .sql files (now they are there), and finally runs the tests, all with the same state. So it did not see citext when it looked for it. To overcome this, I cheated and installed the citext extension on the template1 database. PostgreSQL has 3 databases that it comes with. postgres stores global stuff, like user accounts. template0 is a bare database. template1 is what new databases are created from. So when the unit tests create the voat database, citext is present when it is looked for, and the CREATE EXTENSION in the .sql file becomes redundant. This is only an issue for the tests. You should not have this issue when deploying the application because the library state is presumably refreshed between the database creation and when the application starts. Note that the template databases are hidden and you have to show system objects in your GUI if you want to browse to them.

The second problem was that you added the public schema to the search_path in only the data .sql file, and not the users .sql file, and then pointed both to the same database. The alter search_path sets dbo,public on the voat database, and because the users .sql file also points to the same voat database, alter search_path sets it to dbo, removing the public schema reference. This causes the server to send back public.citext instead of citext, which the library does not recognize. This is only an issue if you point users and data to the same database. You would not have this issue when deploying the application to 2 separate databases.

I added another commit and pull request. It currently fails if you remove citext from the template1 database, but there is a solution.

All schema objects are given OIDs (Object Identifiers). It is just an integer primary key for the object. It is a sequence. Each time that you create a custom type, you almost always get a different OID.

In /test/Voat.Tests/AssemblyInit.cs, you have: 

//Force configuration
var x = db.Ad.FirstOrDefault();

I think what is happening is that this causes EntityFramework to cache the citext OID from the database that is about to get dropped. Then TestDataInitializer.InitializeDatabase drops the database, creates the citext extension with a different OID, and then when EntityFramework tries to reference a citext field on the new database for a test, it says that it cannot find the old OID.

You can choose one of the following solutions:

  1. Comment out "var x = db.Ad.FirstOrDefault();" to prevent the old value from going into the cache.
  2. Find the cache that stores this and clear it. NpgsqlConnection.ReloadTypes is not enough. I think that it also has to be cleared in EntityFramework somewhere.
  3. Put citext in template1, and the OID is the same for every new database that you create going forward. Note that you will get test failures on the first test run, but subsequent test runs will work.

The "ALTER TABLE t ALTER COLUMN c TYPE t" command works, but you also want to add the check constraint at the same time. Also, foreign keys have to be dropped during the alter process because you cannot alter both sides of a foreign key at once, and they need to be the same data type. Most keys tend to be integers, but you will need to do this for the text foreign keys.

The problem is that once you allow case sensitive data into a primary key or a unique constraint, you are going to have duplicate key errors. So when/if you migrate from SQL Server to PostgreSQL, you want every text field using citext from the very beginning of write activity, or you may have headaches dealing with all sorts of duplicate keys when you find stuff that was not case insensitive and should have been. I think that we are going to have that problem with the current preview site, given the bug reports. But if you select the right tables, or manually fix the data, then you should be fine.

The following SQL automates the process of saving off the foreign keys, dropping them, adding the check constraints, altering the types, and recreating the foreign keys. This will probably fail on the problem columns. Fortunately, error reporting is very good in PostgreSQL, so you should be able to see the data that is causing you issues in the error message and hints. Also, this script will change all varchar fields in a table. In practice, you should do the entire database at once unless if you get lucky. If you select which tables you want to convert, and those have foreign key relationships using varchar types, then you will have to include both sides of that relationship. For example, to convert Badge, you also have to convert UserBadge. When you add that other side, you might pick up yet more relationships that will be required, because now every column in that new table will get converted and it may have additional relationships with varchars.

BEGIN;

DO $$
DECLARE
 recreate_fk_sql TEXT;
BEGIN
 SELECT COALESCE(string_agg('ALTER TABLE "'||nspname||'"."'||relname||'" ADD CONSTRAINT "'||conname||'" '|| pg_get_constraintdef(pg_constraint.oid), E';\n'), '')
 INTO recreate_fk_sql
 FROM pg_constraint
 INNER JOIN pg_class ON conrelid = pg_class.oid
 INNER JOIN pg_namespace ON pg_namespace.oid = pg_class.relnamespace
 WHERE pg_constraint.contype = 'f' AND
 ( pg_class.relname IN ('UserPreference','Badge','UserBadge') OR
 replace(pg_constraint.confrelid::regclass::text, '"', '') IN ('UserPreference','Badge','UserBadge')
 );

 EXECUTE (
 SELECT COALESCE(string_agg('ALTER TABLE "'||nspname||'"."'||relname||'" DROP CONSTRAINT "'||conname||E'";\n', ''), '')
 FROM pg_constraint
 INNER JOIN pg_class ON conrelid=pg_class.oid
 INNER JOIN pg_namespace ON pg_namespace.oid=pg_class.relnamespace
 WHERE pg_constraint.contype = 'f' AND
 ( pg_class.relname IN ('UserPreference','Badge','UserBadge') OR
 replace(pg_constraint.confrelid::regclass::text, '"', '') IN ('UserPreference','Badge','UserBadge')
 )
 );

 EXECUTE (SELECT string_agg(format('ALTER TABLE %s ADD CONSTRAINT %I CHECK (char_length(%I::text) <= %s)',
 a.attrelid::regclass, a.attname || '_check', a.attname, substring(format_type(a.atttypid, a.atttypmod) from 19 for length(format_type(a.atttypid, a.atttypmod)) - 19)), E';\n')
FROM pg_attribute a JOIN
 pg_class c ON c.oid = a.attrelid JOIN
 pg_namespace n ON n.oid = c.relnamespace
WHERE c.relkind = 'r' AND
 a.atttypid IN ('varchar'::regtype) AND
 format_type(a.atttypid, a.atttypmod) NOT IN ('character varying') AND
 NOT a.attisdropped AND
 a.attnum > 0 AND
 n.nspname NOT LIKE ALL ('{pg_%, information_schema}'::text[]) AND
 c.relname IN ('UserPreference','Badge','UserBadge'));

 EXECUTE (SELECT string_agg(format('ALTER TABLE %s ALTER COLUMN %I TYPE citext',
 a.attrelid::regclass, a.attname), E';\n')
FROM pg_attribute a JOIN
 pg_class c ON c.oid = a.attrelid JOIN
 pg_namespace n ON n.oid = c.relnamespace
WHERE c.relkind = 'r' AND
 a.atttypid IN ('varchar'::regtype, 'text'::regtype) AND
 NOT a.attisdropped AND
 a.attnum > 0 AND
 n.nspname NOT LIKE ALL ('{pg_%, information_schema}'::text[]) AND
 c.relname IN ('UserPreference','Badge','UserBadge'));

 EXECUTE recreate_fk_sql;
END $$;

COMMIT;

Removing the non-min duplicate keys:

BEGIN;

DELETE FROM ci_table
WHERE EXISTS (
 SELECT ci_table_min.key::citext
 FROM ci_table AS ci_table_min
 WHERE ci_table_min.key::citext = ci_table.key::citext
 GROUP BY ci_table_min.key::citext
 HAVING COUNT(*) > 1) AND
 ci_table.key NOT IN (
 SELECT min(ci_table_min.key)
 FROM ci_table AS ci_table_min
 WHERE ci_table_min.key::citext = ci_table.key::citext
 GROUP BY ci_table_min.key::citext
 HAVING COUNT(*) > 1);

EDIT: here's why not to use it for non-Stormer purposes.

"When using Tor to connect to a hidden service (such as 6zdgh5a5e6zpchdz.onion or facebookcorewwwi.onion) your connection is protected by end-to-end encryption between your Tor client and the hidden service.

When you connect via Web2Tor, the Web2Tor instance sits between you and the hidden service, occupying a very privileged position that not only allows it to see what you're doing, but also to modify and inject content (see below for an example of that).

Because of the way Web2Tor works, you will also disclose the hidden service you're visiting to a wider audience. When you try and access 6zdgh5a5e6zpchdz.onion.cab, your system sends out a DNS query, meaning that your ISP (and others) can see the hidden service you intend on visiting.

Others on the route between you and the Web2Tor instance can also see which Hidden service you're trying to access. Even if the Web2Tor instance is using HTTPS (not all do), the domain you're trying to visit is included within your browser's SSL handshake (known as the Server Name Identification extension).

So, by connecting to a hidden service via a Web2Tor instance, not only have you given a third-party opportunity to interfere with your connection, you've also announced which hidden service you're visiting to an unknown audience."
